title: Language Endangerment & Revitalization

pts: A substantial proportion of the world's languages are considered endangered, with meaningful numbers facing potential extinction within coming generations.
This is a genuinely significant linguistic and cultural loss, distinct from but related to the language-policy questions raised in Unit 71.
Understanding this scale contextualises the specific role English's global spread plays within this larger picture.

v: A simplified version of UNESCO’s vitality factors (written for this book)

items: Choose a language spoken in or near your district that is not taught in school, with care and respect for its speakers.
Using simplified vitality questions, find out: Do children learn it at home? How many speakers are there? In which places is it used? Is it written? Are there materials?
Gather information from reliable sources and, with permission, from community members.
Place the language on a six-point scale from ‘safe’ to ‘extinct’.
Discuss what the scale can and cannot capture about a living community.
With teachers, compare two languages from different parts of India.
Support: provide a completed example for one language.
Challenge: learners compare figures from two sources and explain any differences.

blocks.x: Simplified vitality questions (written for this book, based on the factors in UNESCO 2003):

lines: Do most children in the community learn the language at home?
Is it used at home only, or also at markets, festivals and on the phone?
Are there books, songs, radio or videos in the language?
How do speakers feel about their language?

blocks.x: Figures on numbers of languages and speakers vary between sources, because counting depends on how a ‘language’ is defined. The 2011 Census of India, for example, recorded thousands of mother-tongue names, later grouped into 121 languages [VERIFY figures].

body: Purpose: to show degrees of endangerment. Content: a six-step staircase from ‘safe’ down to ‘extinct’, each step with a family icon showing which generations still speak the language. Style: respectful, clear. Board version: six steps with labels.

items: UNESCO World Atlas of Languages (free online) and Ethnologue (limited free access) for information. [VERIFY current access]

blocks.x: A printed simplified vitality sheet and interviews with community members.

pts: English's global spread is one factor, among several, contributing to language shift away from smaller, local languages in some contexts.
This connects directly to Unit 59's linguistic-imperialism debate — this is one of the concrete phenomena that debate addresses.
This isn't a reason to reject English teaching, but it is a reason for genuine awareness of this broader dynamic.

items: Learners interview a grandparent, a parent and themselves (or other family members of different ages) about which languages they use at home, with friends, at work or school, and on the phone.
They complete a grid for each generation.
In groups, they look for patterns: which languages are growing, which shrinking, and where?
The class discusses reasons: schooling, jobs, migration, media, marriage.
Learners write a paragraph in English, and optionally in their home language, about their family’s language story.
Collect the grids anonymously to make a class chart of language shift across generations.
Support: a picture-based grid for younger learners.
Challenge: learners compare their findings with published descriptions of language shift (Fishman 1991).

blocks.x: A learner’s paragraph (written for this book):

lines: My grandmother speaks Tulu at home and Kannada at the market. My mother speaks Tulu with her mother but Kannada with us. I understand Tulu but I answer in Kannada, and I use English on my phone. My little cousin knows only a few Tulu words.
T: What changed between your grandmother and your cousin?
S1: The language at home. At school we need Kannada and English.
T: Is English the only reason?
S2: No. Kannada is also important for jobs here.

body: Purpose: to show shift across generations. Content: a family tree with three generations, each person surrounded by coloured language labels whose size shows how much they use each. Style: warm, personal. Board version: three rows of stick figures with language names.

items: Google Forms (free) for an anonymous class survey.

blocks.x: A printed grid completed at home.

pts: Language revitalization movements work to document, teach, and restore intergenerational transmission of endangered languages.
Some revitalization programmes draw directly on language-teaching methodology this series has covered — immersion, task-based learning, materials development.
This connects skills from this entire series to a genuinely different, valuable application beyond English teaching specifically.

items: Read short descriptions of two revitalization approaches: the language nest, in which young children are cared for in the endangered language, and the master–apprentice model, in which a fluent elder and a learner spend many hours together using only the language (Hinton and Hale 2001).
Identify which methods from this book they use: immersion, task-based learning, comprehensible input, materials development.
In groups, plan one 20-minute task-based session to teach a community language to young children, with an elder as the language expert and a teacher as the planner.
Discuss the teacher’s role: supporting, not controlling, the community’s own decisions.
Invite a speaker of a local minority language to comment on the plan.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A session outline (written for this book):

lines: Task: plant seeds in the school garden. The elder names tools and actions in the language; children repeat, then follow spoken instructions. No English or state language is used.
Methods: total physical response, task-based learning, comprehensible input.
A: This is just like our English lessons, but in reverse.
B: Yes. The same skills serve any language.

body: Purpose: to show transferable methods. Content: a teacher’s toolbox labelled with methods (tasks, input, stories, songs, materials), from which arrows go to English and to an endangered language. Style: clear. Board version: a box with two arrows.

items: Audacity (free, open source) to record elders’ songs and stories with consent.

blocks.x: Story cards and objects prepared with community members.

body: Māori ‘language nests’ (Kōhanga Reo) in New Zealand, begun in the 1980s, inspired similar programmes elsewhere, including Hawaiian-language preschools (Hinton and Hale 2001).

points.h: English Teaching and Local Language Support
pts: Some contexts successfully support both robust English education and strong local-language maintenance, especially through additive bilingual models (Unit 88).
This isn't an inevitable trade-off — thoughtful policy and programme design can support both goals simultaneously.
This connects directly to Unit 88's additive-versus-subtractive-bilingualism distinction, applied at a broader societal scale.

v: School walk; notebooks; the school timetable

items: Walk around the school and record every language visible: signs, notices, displays, textbooks.
Note where learners’ home languages appear and where they are absent.
Check how home languages are treated in lessons: welcomed, tolerated or banned.
Classify school practices as additive (adding English to existing languages) or subtractive (replacing them) (Unit 88).
Propose two changes that support home languages without reducing English.
Learners photograph (with permission) and label the school’s linguistic landscape.
Support: provide a checklist of places to look.
Challenge: compare with a multilingual education programme such as those in Odisha.

blocks.x: A language map summary (written for this book):

lines: Signs: Kannada and English. Textbooks: Kannada and English. Home languages of learners: Kannada, Urdu, Tamil, Lambani. Lambani appears nowhere in the school.
Proposed changes: a welcome board in all learners’ languages; home-language planning allowed in English writing (Unit 71).

blocks.x: Additive models show that strong English and strong home languages need not be a trade-off.

body: Purpose: to contrast additive and subtractive bilingualism. Content: two jars; in one, English is poured on top of the home language, filling it higher; in the other, the home language is poured out as English goes in. Style: simple metaphor. Board version: two jars.

items: Google Slides (free) for a photo map of the school.

blocks.x: A hand-drawn map of the school with languages marked.

points.h: A Teacher's Role in This Landscape
pts: Individual English teachers aren't typically positioned to resolve these large, systemic policy questions alone.
Genuine awareness of this broader context nonetheless supports more thoughtful, less unreflectively triumphalist professional practice.
This connects directly to Unit 59's critical-language-awareness stance — informed, not guilt-driven, professional awareness.

items: Sort statements about English into three piles: ‘triumphalist’, ‘guilt-driven’ and ‘informed’.
Discuss borderline cases.
Rewrite each triumphalist and guilt-driven statement as an informed one.
Choose one informed statement to guide your teaching this term.
Use the statements as a reading-and-discussion task with B2–C1 learners.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Triumphalist: English is the language of the future; other languages are for the home.
Guilt-driven: By teaching English I am destroying my learners’ languages.
Informed: English gives my learners real opportunities; I can teach it in ways that value and use their other languages.
T: Which statement helps you teach better tomorrow?
A: The informed one. The others either ignore the problem or leave me with nothing to do.

blocks.x: Critical language awareness (Unit 59) aims at this informed stance.

body: Purpose: to show the informed stance. Content: a path between two cliffs labelled ‘triumph’ and ‘guilt’, with a teacher walking the middle path labelled ‘informed awareness’. Style: calm. Board version: a line between two slopes.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for an anonymous card sort.

pts: Most of the world's population is multilingual, with English typically added to, rather than replacing, an existing linguistic repertoire.
This connects to Unit 71's translanguaging pedagogy — most learners this series addresses are genuinely multilingual, not monolingual English learners.
This reframing counters a sometimes implicit, English-centric framing this series' own subject matter could otherwise encourage.

items: Give each learner a body outline.
Learners choose a colour for each language or dialect they know, even partly, and colour the body wherever it ‘lives’ for them (head, heart, hands).
They explain their portrait to a partner in English, using their home language where needed.
Display the portraits and count the languages in the class.
Discuss: in this class, is being multilingual unusual or normal?
Teachers make their own portraits in a workshop to reflect on their repertoires.
Support: provide sentence frames.
Challenge: learners write a paragraph about one language’s place in their life.

lines: I speak ___ with ___. I coloured it on my ___ because ___.

blocks.x: A learner’s explanation (written for this book):

lines: S1: Urdu is in my heart because my grandmother speaks it. Kannada is in my hands because I use it with friends. English is in my head because I study it.

blocks.x: Language portraits are a well-established way to explore linguistic repertoires (Busch 2012). Most of the world’s people use more than one language (Grosjean 2010), and most learners reading this book are multilingual too.

body: Purpose: to model the activity. Content: a child’s body outline coloured in several colours, each labelled with a language (e.g. Urdu on the heart, Kannada on the hands, English on the head). Style: childlike, colourful. Board version: a simple outline with labels.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable template.

body: Accept every variety learners name, including dialects and languages they only half know. The purpose is to show the richness of the repertoire, not to test language labels.

pts: Corpus-linguistics techniques (Unit 58) and digital tools (Unit 18) increasingly support endangered-language documentation efforts too.
This connects methodological skills from throughout this series to valuable applications beyond English-teaching specifically.
This is a genuinely hopeful, active area where linguistic and technological skill converge for language preservation.

items: With community leaders’ permission, learners choose a theme, such as farming tools, festival foods or kinship terms.
They record elders saying words and short phrases in the community language, with informed consent.
They build a trilingual word bank: community language, state language and English, with pictures.
Learners present the word bank to the community and give copies to the school library.
Discuss who owns the material and how it may be shared.
Collect short stories or songs instead of words.
Support: work on ten words in pairs.
Challenge: learners annotate a short recording with a transcription and translation.

dek: Unit 94 of 100: closing this stretch of Tier IV by connecting ELT to the wider linguistic landscape — including the real cost English's spread sometimes carries for other languages.

aims.x: This book is about teaching English, but English is one language among roughly seven thousand, and its spread has consequences for the others. This unit widens the frame. It looks at language endangerment, at English as one factor in language shift, and at the revitalization movements that use many of the teaching methods this book has described. The aim is not guilt or paralysis, but informed awareness: English teachers in multilingual India are well placed to support learners’ other languages while teaching English well.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe the scale of language endangerment globally and in India, using sources carefully;
explain language shift and the part English can play in it, alongside other factors;
describe revitalization approaches and the teaching methods they draw on;
explain how additive bilingual programmes can support both English and local languages;
take an informed, non-triumphalist stance towards English in your own practice;
use activities that present multilingualism as the norm;
support community language documentation with simple, ethical digital tools.

why: Why this matters. English teaching doesn't happen in isolation from the world's broader linguistic ecology, where many languages face genuine, serious endangerment.

background.x: In 1992 the linguist Michael Krauss warned that a large proportion of the world’s languages were no longer being learned by children and could cease to be spoken within this century (Krauss 1992). Since then, UNESCO has developed a framework of nine factors for assessing language vitality, the most important being whether children still learn the language at home (UNESCO Ad Hoc Expert Group on Endangered Languages 2003), and its Atlas of the World’s Languages in Danger lists thousands of endangered languages, with India among the countries with the largest number (Moseley 2010) [VERIFY count for India]. NEP 2020 itself notes that many Indian languages are endangered and calls for their protection and promotion (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020) [VERIFY paragraph].

Languages rarely die because speakers choose to abandon them freely. Language shift happens when economic, educational and social pressures make another language seem necessary for a child’s future. Joshua Fishman (1991) showed that the decisive stage is the break in transmission between parents and children, and that revitalization must restore that transmission, not only teach the language in school. English is one pressure among several; in India, dominant regional languages such as Hindi, Kannada or Odia can also draw speakers away from tribal and minority languages. Robert Phillipson (1992) argued that English spreads through structural inequalities, a debate introduced in Unit 59.

India also offers positive models. Ajit Mohanty (2006) described Indian multilingualism as often ‘unequal’, with tribal children disadvantaged when schooling ignores their home languages, and multilingual education programmes in Odisha and elsewhere have begun schooling in children’s home languages before adding the state language and English. NEP 2020 recommends teaching in the home language or mother tongue, wherever possible, at least until Grade 5 (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and the Central Institute of Indian Languages in Mysuru runs a scheme for documenting endangered languages [VERIFY scheme name and status]. English teachers who value learners’ home languages are part of this effort, not outside it.

items: Vitality check. A careful, sourced description of one language’s vitality, with limitations noted.
Language shift study. A three-generation survey with an analysis of patterns and causes.
School language map. An audit of additive and subtractive practices, with two proposed changes.
Professional statement. A short statement of how you position English within your learners’ repertoires.
Which languages in your learners’ lives are growing, and which are shrinking?
How is each home language treated in your classroom?
When have you been triumphalist, or guilt-driven, about English?
What could your school do to support a local minority language?
How would you respond to a parent who wants the school to use only English?
What does it mean to you to be multilingual?

perm: Family information is personal; learners share only what they and their families are comfortable sharing.
Recordings of community members require informed consent; communities retain ownership of their language materials.

All vitality questions, learner paragraphs, session outlines, statements and word-bank entries are written for this book; the people named are fictional. Screenshots of the UNESCO Atlas, Ethnologue, Audacity, ELAN, Wikitongues, Padlet, Canva or Google tools require permission or replacement with original illustrations. terms.def: The learning of a second language while the first language continues to be valued and developed, so that the learner gains a language rather than replacing one; for example, adding English to Kannada rather than substituting it.
The passing of a language from parents to children in the home. Its breakdown is the most important sign that a language is endangered.
Recording and archiving a language, including audio and video of speakers, texts, dictionaries and grammars, especially for endangered languages, so that they can be studied, taught and revitalized.
The situation in which a language is at risk of no longer being spoken, usually because children are no longer learning it (Krauss 1992).
An early childhood programme in which young children are cared for entirely in an endangered language, as in the Māori Kōhanga Reo in New Zealand (Hinton and Hale 2001).
The process by which a community gradually replaces one language with another in more and more domains, often over generations.
The strength of a language in terms of its use and transmission, assessed by factors such as whether children still learn it at home (UNESCO Ad Hoc Expert Group on Endangered Languages 2003).
The whole set of languages, dialects, registers and styles that a person can draw on; a learner in Bengaluru may use Kannada, Tamil, Hindi and English for different purposes.
A language revitalization approach in which a fluent speaker, often an elder, and a learner spend many hours together using only the endangered language in everyday activities (Hinton and Hale 2001).

Organized efforts to reverse language shift and increase the use of an endangered language, for example through community classes, mother-tongue schooling, recording elders and creating new materials. Many draw on familiar language-teaching methods.
